item.title: Arvell Reese wins first NFC defensive player of the week award
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese was all over the field in Sunday's victory over the Eagles.
item.content:encoded:
Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese was all over the field in Sunday's victory over the Eagles.

The league has now recognized his performance, naming him NFC defensive player of the week.

This is Reese's first career player of the week award.

Reese finished the contest with 12 tackles, 3.0 sacks, and a forced fumble in the 19-11 victory over Philadelphia.

According to the league, Reese became the youngest player since 1982 — when the sack became an official stat — to have at least three sacks in a game. Reese is 21 years and 70 days old. The previous record holder was Vernon Maxwell, who was 21 years and 321 days old on Sept. 11, 1983.

The No. 5 overall pick in this year’s draft, Reese has tallied 68 total tackles, 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for loss, and an interception so far this season.

item.title: C.J. Stroud named AFC offensive player of the week for second time this season
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Texans quarterback C.J.
item.content:encoded:
Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud didn't sign a contract extension ahead of the 2026 season and that set him up for a prove-it year in Houston.

Last Sunday's game against the Chargers was one Stroud can use to make his case for a new deal. Stroud threw five touchdowns as the Texans picked up a 44-22 win in Los Angeles.

Stroud was 21-of-35 for 384 yards overall and he added a pair of runs for 20 yards. The NFL named Stroud the AFC offensive player of the week on Wednesday.

It's the second time this season and fifth time overall that Stroud received the award. He has 2,251 passing yards, 16 touchdowns and two interceptions while completing 64.2 percent of his passes so far this year.

item.title: Jordan Love wins fifth career NFC offensive player of the week award
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Jordan Love has been outstanding throughout the 2026 season, but he had an especially strong game against the Patriots on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Jordan Love has been outstanding throughout the 2026 season, but he had an especially strong game against the Patriots on Sunday.

Now the Packers’ quarterback has been named offensive player of the week for the first time in 2026.

Love finished the 45-27 victory 23-of-29 passing for 372 yards with three touchdowns and zero interceptions. He also had a rushing touchdown.

Love’s 153.2 passer rating was No. 1 in the league for Week 9 and his 372 passing yards along with a 79.3 completion rate led the conference.

This is the fifth career offensive player of the week award for Love, who last won it for his Week 13 performance last season.

Love and the Packers will host the division-rival Vikings in Week 10.

item.title: Jaguars designate DE B.J. Green for return
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Jaguars have welcomed three new players to the team this week and they will also be reintegrating a current member of the team into practice.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaguars have welcomed three new players to the team this week and they will also be reintegrating a current member of the team into practice.

The team announced on Wednesday that they have designated defensive end B.J. Green for return from injured reserve. Green suffered an elbow injury in the first game of the season.

Green played three special teams snaps in that game. He joined the Jags as an undrafted free agent in 2025 and appeared in 14 games. He had 15 tackles, two sacks and a fumble recovery.

The Jaguars will have a 21-day window to activate Green and he'll be ineligible to return this season if he does not rejoin the active roster before that period is over.

item.title: Report: Despite multiple offers, Colts will not trade Jonathan Taylor
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: It turns out Jonathan Taylor will not be on the move.
item.content:encoded:
It turns out Jonathan Taylor will not be on the move.

According to Tom Pelissero of Netflix, the Colts will not trade Taylor prior to the 4 p.m. ET deadline on Tuesday.

Pelissero notes that while multiple teams offered a second-round pick and more for the running back, the Colts “wanted a blockbuster offer to even consider it.”

It’s worth noting there is still time for the Colts to receive such an offer before the deadline this afternoon.

Since firing former General Manager Chris Ballard, Indianapolis has made several moves with an eye toward the future — including dealing receiver Keenan Allen to San Francisco earlier on Tuesday.

The Colts also reportedly informed quarterback Daniel Jones that he will not be traded prior to the deadline.

The Titans have added a linebacker.

item.title: Miami of Ohio penalized for Patriots-style video board trickery on field goal attempt
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: At the start of this season, a former NFL analytics staffer publicized a longstanding effort by the Patriots to confuse opposing kickers with the video board behind the goal posts, showing an image of the goal posts meant to cause an optical illusion and make it harder for a kicker to put the ball through the uprights.
item.content:encoded:
At the start of this season, a former NFL analytics staffer publicized a longstanding effort by the Patriots to confuse opposing kickers with the video board behind the goal posts, showing an image of the goal posts meant to cause an optical illusion and make it harder for a kicker to put the ball through the uprights. At the time the Patriots were doing it, it was legal. Shortly after it was revealed, the NFL banned it.

Miami of Ohio found out on Tuesday night that it's not legal in college football, either.

Just before halftime of its game against Ohio, as Ohio lined up for a field goal, the Miami video board operator put images of goal posts on the video board, in the line of the Ohio kicker's vision, in an attempt to confuse the visiting kicker. The referee threw a flag and announced that it was unsportsmanlike conduct.

"On the previous play, there were depictions of the field goal uprights on the scoreboard. That is a foul for unsportsmanlike conduct against Miami. Half the distance to the goal, automatic first down," the referee said.

Ohio accepted the penalty and attempted to score a touchdown with two seconds remaining in the half on the next play, but the Miami defense held, so the penalty didn't really cost Miami. And Miami ultimately won the game 34-17, so nothing about that play ultimately had an impact on the final result.

Miami head coach Chuck Martin said after the game that he had no idea his team could get penalized for what was shown on the video board.

"We get the scoreboard penalty," Martin said. "I didn't even know there was such a thing."

Many people didn't know there was such a penalty. Now they know.

item.title: Colts mishandled the Jonathan Taylor situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When the dust settled on the trade deadline, the Colts still had running back Jonathan Taylor under contract.
item.content:encoded:
When the dust settled on the trade deadline, the Colts still had running back Jonathan Taylor under contract. It was not the outcome that most around the league expected.

All signs pointed to the Colts taking the best offer at 3:45 p.m. ET and processing the paperwork before the top of the hour. Whatever the best offer was.

But that's what a functional organization would have done. The Colts currently are not.

The Giants were willing to give up a second-round pick and a fifth-round pick for Taylor. It's unclear for now whether anyone else was willing to do better than that.

In the interim, Taylor spent two weeks not knowing what would happen. He didn't get an assurance he wouldn't be traded until roughly an hour before the window closed. (Even then, the leak felt more like a "last call" to interested suitors.)

The fans spent that same period of time wondering what the Colts were doing. And Taylor got only eight carries in the 42-7 loss to Jacksonville, at a time when it felt like a trade was imminent.

So what happens next for Taylor? If they try to trade him in the offseason, they won't do better than they would have done when a contender was willing to pay a premium in an effort to win now. And if they don't get at least as much as they could have gotten on Tuesday, will they refuse to trade him again?

Taylor could end up being stuck on the Colts during an obvious rebuild. Then, by the time it's rebuilt (if it ever is), Taylor will be past his prime.

The simplest explanation is that the Colts slipped into dysfunction on this one. And it's no surprise. Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is still fairly new to the job. The G.M. has been fired. And coach Shane Steichen hopes to win enough games to have a chance to keep his job; he surely wasn't lobbying to lose his best player.

So what should the Colts have done? When they were doing the deals for guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, they should have asked for the various Taylor suitors to make their last, best offers. And the Colts should have made a final decision then and there as to whether he'd be traded or retained.

Instead, they decided to wait and see whether the offers would improve. Taylor was left to wonder about his future. After the Week 9 loss to the Cowboys, he basically said goodbye to Indianapolis.

The Eagles didn't play it that way with running back Saquon Barkley. They knew what was out there, they decided not to take the best offer, and they informed Barkley that he wouldn't be changing teams.

The Colts instead kicked the can, not accepting the best offer and hoping it would impove. That gave Taylor two weeks to ponder the possibility of playing for a contender before the Colts decided not to pull the trigger on a trade.

They'll never admit it, but the Colts will come to regret not taking the best deal. Because the offers won't get any better after the season. At some point, Taylor is going to realize it's in his best interests to request a trade.

That will be a problem for the next G.M. to deal with. And that wrinkle won't make the job more attractive to a candidate who has options.

item.title: Report: Giants called Falcons about a potential Bijan Robinson trade
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Giants didn't make any big deals at the trade deadline, but they tried to make a very big one.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants didn't make any big deals at the trade deadline, but they tried to make a very big one.

The Giants called the Falcons to see whether running back Bijan Robinson was available in a trade, according to Jordan Raanan of ESPN.

That would have been a blockbuster, but it's unsurprising that the teams didn't make a deal. The Falcons made a big investment in Robinson this offseason, signing him to a three-year, $66.8 million contract extension, and from all accounts they view him as one of the most important pieces of their franchise.

There's no word on what the Giants were willing to offer, or whether the Falcons engaged at all, or simply told the Giants, "Not interested."

The Giants did make one big trade this season, acquiring J.J. McCarthy, who has played well enough for the Giants to win their first two starts and remain in first place in the NFC East. Acquiring Robinson would have been a strong sign that the Giants believe they're serious contenders, this year. That the Giants even tried showed that coach John Harbaugh meant it when he said they're a team trying to win now, not build for the future.

item.title: John Spytek: Fernando Mendoza passed every test, allowed us to make a hard decision
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: It took longer than it has for most quarterbacks drafted first overall, but Fernando Mendoza's time has come in Las Vegas.
item.content:encoded:
It took longer than it has for most quarterbacks drafted first overall, but Fernando Mendoza's time has come in Las Vegas.

Tuesday's trade of Kirk Cousins means that Mendoza is now the No. 1 quarterback for the Raiders and he'll make his first NFL start in Sunday's game against the Seahawks. The Raiders went into the season determined to give Mendoza as much time as possible to learn from Cousins and their 4-5 start made it possible to stick with the plan rather than turn attention to the future.

The move would have waited a little while longer if the Vikings were not motivated buyers in the wake of Monday night's disastrous performance against the Bills, but General Manager John Spytek said at a Tuesday press conference that the trade would not have happened without Mendoza showing the team that he's ready.

“It’s something that he’s worked very hard for since the moment he walked into this building," Spytek said. "He passed every test. I want to stop short of saying he’s earned it, but he put us in a position where we had to make a really hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback."

While the Raiders feel Mendoza is ready, it is a big change to go from the practice field to game action and the Seahawks are a tough first opponent for the rookie. The Raiders drafted Mendoza to be their leader, however, and head coach Klint Kubiak said Mendoza has "exceeded those expectations" while learning from a good teacher.

"I think with the right role model that will accelerate his growth and we had, you know, we had the right role model," Kubiak said.

Becoming the starter is just the beginning for Mendoza and it kicks off an era the Raiders hope will bring them back to the upper rungs of the AFC in the years to come.

item.title: PFT's Week 10 2026 NFL power rankings
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Bills benefit from facing another backup QB.
item.content:encoded:
1. Bills (last week No. 1; 7-1): If they'd been playing a team with a borderline functional offense, they may have surrendered the top spot to Jacksonville.

2. Jaguars (No. 2; 6-2): Who cares about future draft picks when the AI apocalypse is coming?

3. 49ers (No. 3; 7-1): It feels like they'll be up to something on trade-deadline day.

4. Broncos (No. 4; 7-2): They're good enough to win the games they try to lose.

5. Bears (No. 5; 7-2): Caleb Williams isn't trying to become Patrick Mahomes; he's hoping to morph into Michael Jordan.

6. Chiefs (No. 7; 6-2): The kicker position shouldn't be a pick-your-poison proposition.

7. Steelers (No. 8; 6-2): Completing the sweep of the Bengals will be critical to winning the division.

8. Bengals (No. 11; 6-2): A Super Bowl push is very realistic.

9. Seahawks (No. 9; 5-4): Drew Lock fits this team better than Sam Darnold does.

10. Lions (No. 12; 6-2): What's German for kneecap?

11. Packers (No. 14; 6-3): When Micah Parsons returns, they could make a major move.

12. Vikings (No. 6; 6-2): Tuesday is arguably the most pivotal non-game day for the Vikings in years; will they upgrade at quarterback?

13. Giants (No. 16; 5-2-1): They're gradually pulling away in the NFC East.

14. Patriots (No. 10; 5-4): The regression continues.

15. Rams (No. 15; 5-4): Can Ty Simpson play receiver?

16. Browns (No. 13; 5-4): Can they stop the bleeding?

17. Raiders (No. 17; 4-5): It's time to flip the Fernando switch.

18. Buccaneers (No. 18; 3-6): They'd be dangerous on the road in the playoffs, if they can get there.

19. Ravens (No. 19; 4-5): Can they hold it together until Lamar Jackson returns?

20. Texans (No. 23; 3-5): C.J. Stroud is earning millions by the week.

21. Saints (No. 25; 3-5): Suddenly, they're tied for first place in the division.

22. Panthers (No. 22; 3-5): David Tepper is going to pull out all the stops in an effort to land Mike Tomlin.

23. Cardinals (No. 20; 3-6): Good news, Carson Beck — you're playing. Bad news, Carson Beck — you're playing.

24. Falcons (No. 21; 3-6): The Jessie Bates trade says it all; they're not interested in winning the division and getting blown out by the No. 5 seed in the wild-card round.

25. Cowboys (No. 26; 4-5): Even the games against the bad teams are a struggle.

26. Commanders (No. 24; 2-5-1): The mini-bye could be the time to bid farewell to the head coach.

27. Eagles (No. 27; 2-7): The soft-shell tank is on.

28. Titans (No. 28; 1-7): No one would have even noticed they were on a bye, but for whatever it was that happened with Calvin Ridley.

29. Colts (No. 29; 2-7): Vaya con dios, Jonathan Taylor.

30. Dolphins (No. 30; 1-7): The only drama left is whether they finish last in the division.

31. Jets (No. 31; 2-7): Same.

32. Chargers (No. 32; 0-8): Do they know they're winless?

item.title: CBA allows 49ers to not pay Brandon Aiyuk during two-week roster exemption
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When unusual situations emerge in the NFL, it becomes a piece-by-piece exercise in figuring out the specific rules that apply.
item.content:encoded:
When unusual situations emerge in the NFL, it becomes a piece-by-piece exercise in figuring out the specific rules that apply. And few situations have been more unusual than 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk's odyssey of the past year.

He's back on the 49ers, at a salary of $13.75 million for the rest of the season. That fact pointed to the 49ers releasing him by 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, in order to avoid owing him one-ninth of the total amount ($1.52 million) for Week 10.

But here's where yet another obscure wrinkle applies. Under Article 20, Section 4 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, the 49ers owe Aiyuk nothing during his two-week roster exemption.

From the relevant provision: "If a Club obtains a roster exemption for a player under contract who does not report to his Club at least five days before the final day of Preseason Training Camp as defined in Article 23, Section 10, the player will not be entitled to preseason or regular season compensation until such exemption is removed, provided the player is given written notice of such fact upon reporting to the Club. If such notice is not given to the player, the player must be paid his Paragraph 5 Salary during his exemption."

So if the 49ers gave Aiyuk written notice that he won't be paid during the two-week roster exemption (and they surely did), they don't have to pay him. Which pushes their deadline for avoiding owing him a game check until Tuesday, November 24 — one day after the expiration of the exemption.

Why not just cut him? The 49ers are delaying the move because they can, postponing by up to two weeks his passage through waivers and, given his salary, inevitable free agency.

In the interim, he's on the team. But Aiyuk won't be reporting for work on Wednesday. He has been excused, we're told, from team activities and he's working out on his own.

The 49ers could release him at any moment. There's no reason not to do so, other than to apply the brakes to his ability to join another team.

The circumstances counter the notion that he was reinstated by the league subject to any type of agreement with the 49ers. If that had happened, the agreement surely would have included a requirement that the 49ers promptly cut him.

Which means that the NFL, after apparently working with the 49ers to delay Aiyuk's reinstatement in order to help the 49ers recover bonus money from Aiyuk, finally decided that reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list can't be delayed in order to advance a team's strategic objectives.

So, yes, Aiyuk eventually will be released. He wasn't released today because the 49ers don't owe him a game check for Week 10, or for Week 11. Eventually, when the roster exemption expires, they'll cut him.

For now, the team's delay in doing the inevitable points to a desire to keep another team from getting him, sticking it to Aiyuk, or some of both. It's petty, but the 49ers have the power to do it.

item.title: Bengals call off trade for Arnold Ebiketie
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Tuesday morning brought word that the Bengals had agreed to acquire pass rusher Arnold Ebiketie in a trade with the Eagles, but that agreement will not be finalized ahead of the 4 p.m.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday morning brought word that the Bengals had agreed to acquire pass rusher Arnold Ebiketie in a trade with the Eagles, but that agreement will not be finalized ahead of the 4 p.m. ET trade deadline.

According to multiple reports, the Bengals have called off the trade and will not be sending a 2027 sixth-round pick to Philadelphia.

The reports surfaced shortly after a tweet by OverTheCap.com contributor Nick Korte explained the compensatory pick ramifications of the deal. According to Korte, who focuses on the compensatory pick system, acquiring Ebiketie would put the Bengals in position to forfeit the third-round compensatory pick that they are currently set to receive for Trey Hendrickson leaving the team to sign with the Ravens.

That would greatly increase the price that the Bengals were going to pay to acquire Ebiketie and it appears they found it too high to move forward with the deal.

item.title: Raiders ended up buying a third-round pick for $650,000
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Did the Raiders get enough for Kirk Cousins?
item.content:encoded:
Did the Raiders get enough for Kirk Cousins?

Some will say no, because the Vikings were desperate to find a quarterback after Monday night's disastrous performance from Carson Wentz. They clearly have no faith in Kyler Murray, and they weren't ready to hand the reins to Max Brosmer. The Raiders had leverage, and it's fair to wonder whether they maximized.

But there's another reality to consider. The Vikings were casting a wide net. They apparently had other options. So if the Raiders had tried to put their thumb on the scale, the Vikings would have gone to a different deli — and the Raiders would have gotten nothing.

They were obviously going to pivot from Cousins to Fernando Mendoza at some point. Possibly, after the Week 13 bye against the Chargers. So they accelerated the plan and got something when they otherwise would have gotten nothing.

Along the way, they avoided the $10 million guaranteed 2027 roster bonus that was engineered to stick the Falcons with $8.7 million of Cousins's $10 million pay for 2026. In the end, the Raiders paid half of Cousins's $1.3 million base salary.

Setting aside the fact that they got nine games out of Cousins (including four wins) and a great mentor for Mendoza, the Raiders ultimately bought a third-round pick for $650,000.

In 2017, the Browns bought a second-round pick from the Texans for $16 million, in the form of taking on Brock Osweiler's remaining salary guarantee under a contract Houston quickly regretted. If a second-round pick was worth $16 million then, how much is a third-round pick worth now?

Whatever it is, it's more than $650,000.

So it was a win for the Raiders. And it was a win for the Vikings.

It also was a win for Cousins, who'll now be the starter for the rest of the season in Minnesota, without having to worry about getting benched for Murray, Wentz, or Brosmer.

item.title: Kirk Cousins isn't officially back in No. 8, yet
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota.
item.content:encoded:
Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota. But he's not back in No. 8. Yet.

The official online roster shows Cousins with no assigned number, for now. The player currently in No. 8 is safety Jakobe Thomas, a third-round pick in the 2026 draft.

It's likely that Thomas — who hasn't played in a 2026 regular-season game — will surrender the number to Cousins. Possibly for an appropriate contribution to the charity of Thomas's choice. Or possibly after Cousins pulls a Jared Verse and shows up for practice on Wednesday wearing No. 8.

There's another possibility, which is as intriguing as it is unlikely. Given that Hall of Famer Fran Tarkenton, who like Cousins had a second stint as Minnesota's starter, is very enthused by the return of Cousins, Tarkenton could offer to temporarily unretire No. 10.

I know. I know. I've made clear my position that retired numbers shouldn't be unretired. More specifically, future players shouldn't initiate the request, since it puts the player for whom the number was retired in a no-win spot. But if the idea comes from the player who holds the permanent rights to the number, that's different.

It's still unlikely. And it would look strange to see Cousins in No. 10. So it makes sense for him to get back in No. 8, and for Thomas to pick one of the other available numbers, like No. 9 (which he wore during his season at Tennessee) or No. 6 (which he wore before that at Middle Tennessee State).

item.title: Browns plan on starting Deshaun Watson against Texans
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Head coach Todd Monken declined to announce a decision earlier this week.
item.content:encoded:
A report on Monday morning indicated that the Browns planned to turn back to Deshaun Watson at quarterback for their Week 10 games against the Texans, but head coach Todd Monken declined to make any announcement during a press conference later in the day.

Monken is scheduled to speak to reporters again on Wednesday and the day opened with multiple reports that Watson will indeed start against his former team. Shedeur Sanders started in last Sunday's loss to the Saints after Watson missed two days of practice while working through the concussion protocol. Watson was cleared on Saturday, but was inactive with Dillon Gabriel serving as the team's No. 2 quarterback.

Sanders was 19-of-31 for 297 yards and two touchdowns before failing to complete a two-point conversion in overtime that would have won the game. Monken said after the game that he was "proud" of the way the quarterback played in his first start of the season, but avoided a question about whether Sanders showed enough to make a case to move up the depth chart permanently.

The Browns offense only generated six points in their Week 8 loss to the Steelers with Watson at the helm and they have a bye in Week 11, so another lackluster outing against Houston could lead to a different decision at quarterback in the future.

UPDATE 9:31 a.m. ET: The Browns have now confirmed that Watson is set to start the game later.

item.title: Vikings announce return of Kirk Cousins
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: It's official.
item.content:encoded:
It's official.

Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota.

The Vikings have announced the trade that brings Cousins from the Raiders for a third-round pick in the 2027 draft. The deal hinges on Cousins passing a physical, which is usually (but not always) a formality.

The Vikings would be out of luck at quarterback if Cousins fails the physical. That will make them far more likely to give it a passing grade.

Cousins spent 2018 through 2023 with the Vikings. His return undoubtedly means he'll become the instant starter, with Carson Wentz undoubtedly being released.

There's no reason to part ways with Kyler Murray. At $1.3 million, he's a low-cost insurance policy, in the event of a Cousins injury. It remains to be seen whether Murray or Max Brosmer will be the primary backup to Cousins.

item.title: John Spytek: First "real" call on Kirk Cousins came this morning
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As NFL trades slip into hibernation until March, it's important to remember something the next time players can be sent from one team to another.
item.content:encoded:
As NFL trades slip into hibernation until March, it's important to remember something the next time players can be sent from one team to another.

Teams push plenty of BS to the media — and the media often passes it along without scrutiny.

Case in point: The internally inconsistent claim made by ESPN on Saturday, undoubtedly based on information straight from the Raiders.

"As of this weekend," Adam Schefter of ESPN tweeted, "the Raiders had not received any trade inquiries regarding their starting quarterback Kirk Cousins, nor are they interested in dealing him, per league sources. They plan to keep sticking with him until they believe their No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza is ready."

So the Raiders hadn't received any trade inquiries, but they weren't interested in the trade inquiries they hadn't received? Right.

In a press conference with reporters on Tuesday, Raiders G.M. John Spytek addressed how it all came to be.

"I never made one call on Kirk Cousins," Spytek said. "And I got a few phone calls. But one real one this morning."

The "real one" ultimately entailed getting a third-round pick for Cousins. Which further highlights how silly it is for a team to claim — and for the media to share — the idea that "WE'RE NOT INTERESTED."

Everyone is interested in a trade offer for all but a small handful of players in the entire league. Anything else is posturing. And, as is often the case when it comes to NFL reporting, the insiders allow themselves to become extensions of the team's P.R. department in an effort to send a given message.

The Raiders weren't interested, until they were. And it didn't take all that much to make them interested in giving up their starting quarterback.

It was easier to make the decision because they were surely thinking about when to bench him for rookie Fernando Mendoza. And it surely was easier for Cousins to embrace the trade, given that he's now in a position to keep playing for a team that has a chance to get to the postseason and to make some noise in January.

item.title: Fran Tarkenton raves about Kirk Cousins's return to Minnesota
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On Monday night, I was explaining to my wife the bizarre situation in Minnesota, where a championship-caliber defense has been paired with an offense that would have trouble scoring a touchdown in the lower divisions of college football.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday night, I was explaining to my wife the bizarre situation in Minnesota, where a championship-caliber defense has been paired with an offense that would have trouble scoring a touchdown in the lower divisions of college football.

She said, "Is Fran Tarkenton still around?"

Actually, he is. And the end result to the expedited search came from the Tarkenton playbook: The Vikings brought back a former Vikings quarterback in trading with the Raiders for Kirk Cousins.

On Tuesday, Tarkenton gushed about the return of Cousins. "I think it's the greatest thing that could have happened to us," Tarkenton told Darren Wolfson of KSTP. "We were lost. We were winning on defense. We had no offense. We had no quarterback. And now we've got Kirk coming back, who is having a great year. He's a great player. He's a better person than player. Our team should lift up now. And we're in the best division in football. Our defense has kept us in the hunt.

"And having Kirk — I cannot tell you how happy I am for the Vikings, for the fans, for the Wilfs, and for all the players and the old-timers like myself. We've got a chance with Kirk Cousins."

Tarkenton spent 1961 through 1966 with the Vikings before returning from 1972 through 1978. And, as it turns out, his comments about Cousins weren't the only news he made this week.

Tarkenton apparently earned a mere $1.2 million during his entire 18-year NFL career. But that was just the starting point. He has amassed enough of a fortune in the business world to recently buy — at age 86 — a $51.89 million home in Palm Beach.

Tarkenton blazed the trail for today's former quarterbacks who work even harder in retirement. He was the first NFL player to host Saturday Night Live, and his TV career included a co-hosting gig on That's Incredible and a four-year stint in the Monday Night Football booth.

The big money came in the business world, specifically computer software. He also has made many millions as an early investor in Apple.

And, if you watch the clip, you'll see that Tarkenton still has a verbal and mental fastball.

The return of Cousins definitely conjures memories of Tarkenton's second act in Minnesota, which resulted in three Super Bowl appearances.

The Vikings would be thrilled if, with Cousins back in the fold, they could manage just one.

item.title: In Kirk Cousins, the Vikings landed their first choice
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After last night's abysmal performance by the offense against the Bills, the Vikings mobilized to trade for a quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
After last night's abysmal performance by the offense against the Bills, the Vikings mobilized to trade for a quarterback. Ultimately, they got the guy they wanted.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, Kirk Cousins was Minnesota's first choice.

The Vikings explored other options. Multiple players, including fellow former Vikings quarterback Daniel Jones.

Cousins's history with the team makes it easier to get him up to speed. He had 25 regular-season games with coach Kevin O'Connell, and four seasons with receiver Justin Jefferson.

The existence of options may have helped the Vikings keep the compensation to only a third-round pick. Given the level of desperation, the Vikings seemed destined to give up more than that to fix a problem that threatened to implode the season.

That's not an overstatement. The dam was breaking. Frustration was rampant during the debacle against the Bills, on both sides of the ball.

It was a simple proposition. If the Vikings didn't trade for a quarterback on Tuesday, they could not be considered a serious franchise.

In the end, they managed to stop the bleeding by sending their third-round pick (their own, not the one they acquired from the Eagles for defensive end Jonathan Greenard) to the Raiders for Cousins.

It's unclear how much better things will be with Cousins back in the fold. It can't get worse than what they put on the field for Week 9.

item.description: The Raiders traded quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Vikings, leaving an open roster spot.
item.content:encoded:
The Raiders traded quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Vikings, leaving an open roster spot. They filled it by signing rookie defensive lineman Tim Keenan to the 53-player roster from the practice squad.

Keenan was out of elevations from the practice squad after the Raiders elevated him for the past three games.

In three games, Keenan totaled seven tackles and a sack while playing 35 percent of the snaps.

The Rams selected Keenan in the seventh round this year out of Alabama. They waived him out of the preseason, but he signed back to their practice squad.

The Raiders signed him to their practice squad on Sept. 7.

The team also announced it signed defensive tackle Chris Williams to the practice squad.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers is one win away from tying Drew Brees for fourth-most of all time
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Steelers' next win will give Rodgers 181 in his career, counting the playoffs, the same number as Brees.
item.content:encoded:
If the Steelers beat the Bengals on Monday night, Aaron Rodgers will move into a tie for fourth place on the NFL's all-time wins list.

Rodgers' teams have won 180 games he has started, counting the playoffs. His next win will give him No. 181, the same number Drew Brees retired with, and the fourth most of all time.

The only quarterbacks in NFL history who have won more starts are Tom Brady with a preposterous 286 wins, Peyton Manning with 200 and Brett Favre with 199. Rodgers has said this will be his last NFL season, so he won't catch Favre for third place.

Rodgers won 158 games as starting quarterback for the Packers, six with the Jets and has now won 16 with the Steelers.

item.title: Commanders GM Adam Peters: Ball needs to go in the end zone on final play
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Commanders' operation at the end of games came under the microscope again in Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
The Commanders' operation at the end of games came under the microscope again in Week 9.

Washington was down 20-13 with the ball at the Rams' 31-yard-line with three seconds left and their final play saw quarterback Jayden Daniels hit tight end Chig Okonkwo with a short pass. Okonkwo got down around the 10 before he attempted to lateral to a teammate. The attempt at a Stanford band-esque ending fizzled out from there and the Commanders fell to 2-5-1 on the season.

The Commanders were in position to lose due to several things that went wrong over the first 59 minutes and 57 seconds of play, but they still had a chance to tie or win the game, which is one that General Manager Adam Peters said they should have taken during a Wednesday appearance on 106.7 The Fan.

"There’s a couple things on that, but I think the bottom line is the ball needs to get in the end zone there," Peters said.

Last Sunday's ending may not have been as egregious an error as the one Daniels and head coach Dan Quinn made at the end of their tie with the Giants, but it was enough of an error that the case for changing those in charge of the on-field operation is even stronger heading into Week 10.

item.title: Jaguars GM James Gladstone: We value draft picks, but don't always use them in April
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Jaguars General Manager James Gladstone doesn't view this week's moves to acquire safety Jessie Bates, defensive tackle Jordan Davis, and defensive tackle Davon Godchaux in the same light as many others around the football world have characterized them.
item.content:encoded:
Jaguars General Manager James Gladstone doesn't view this week's moves to acquire safety Jessie Bates, defensive tackle Jordan Davis, and defensive tackle Davon Godchaux in the same light as many others around the football world have characterized them.

Gladstone sent away the team's 2027 first- and second-round picks, 2028 fifth- and sixth-round picks, and 2029 second-round pick in three Monday trades, which has been positioned as going all-in on maximizing the team's Super Bowl chances after a 6-2 start. In a Tuesday press conference, Gladstone said he wouldn't "necessarily" use the same framing and said he'd describe the team's approach as always "getting better as a football team and prioritizing getting better as a football team."

Another popular response has been that Gladstone has adopted his former Rams boss Les Snead's "F them picks" to building the team's Super Bowl LVI winners and subsequent teams. Gladstone noted that the Rams made plenty of picks while he was there from 2017-2024 and that he always takes into account the compensatory draft pick process during free agency as a way to supplement assets that can be used in a variety of ways.

"It's a very symbiotic process that encompasses a lot of layers to it, but it's certainly not ‘F them picks,’" Gladstone said. "While that's been characterized as the approach, it's not necessarily — we actually value picks. We don't always use them on the three days that exist in April.”

Gladstone also acknowledged that "a part of it" is acquiring known commodities rather than gambling on the unknown trajectories of draft picks. There's a gamble involved with the Jaguars' approach as well and the way it pays off will be a big part of Gladstone's ultimate legacy in Jacksonville.

item.title: Jonah Jackson on Luke Goedeke's grievances: "This is football, man"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After Sunday night's game between the Buccaneers and Bears, Tampa Bay tackle Luke Goedeke had some grievances to air about Chicago defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.
item.content:encoded:
After Sunday night's game between the Buccaneers and Bears, Tampa Bay tackle Luke Goedeke had some grievances to air about Chicago defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Bears guard Jonah Jackson was unpersuaded by Goedeke's complaints about Simmons launching himself at and/or holding Bucs linemen.

"The guys on his team tried to launch themselves at us on every play," Jackson said on 104.3 The Score. "I don't know any different. That's on him how he feels. It is what it is. This is football, man. Especially in the trenches. It gets rough and rowdy. . . . Did you see that big guy, number 50 [Vita Vea], launching at us? . . . It is what it is. We signed up for this."

As to Simmons holding Goedeke, Jackson was equally blunt.

"They all do it. It is what it is. You've got find ways to combat it," he said.

It really is anything goes when it comes to line play, subject to what the officials see and are willing to call. Especially when there are so many uncalled holding penalties on offensive linemen, arguably since defensive ends are so good and the powers-that-be prefer to keep quarterbacks in one piece.

The best, most recent example of that came in Carolina on Sunday, on the play when Broncos linebacker Nik Bonitto forced a fumble by Panthers quarterback Bryce Young to seal the game. Bonitto was being held the entire play. And he still got it done.

That's the message for all offensive and defensive linemen. Do whatever you have to do to get it done. It's only a foul if a flag is thrown.

item.title: Rams more likely to miss the playoffs than make the playoffs, according to betting odds
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: After opening the season as the betting favorites to win the Super Bowl, the Rams are now underdogs to make the playoffs.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams entered the season as the overwhelming favorites to win the Super Bowl. As the dust settles on the NFL trade deadline, the Rams are now not even favored to make the playoffs.

The latest betting odds have the Rams as -130 favorites to miss the playoffs, and +110 underdogs to make the playoffs.

That represents a massive shift from before the season, when the Rams were -500 favorites to make the playoffs, the best playoff odds of any team in the league.

The Rams are a disappointing 5-4, and if the playoffs started today they'd be a game behind the Packers for the third and final NFC playoff spot. They're also 2.5 games behind the 49ers in the NFC West race.

Perhaps more importantly, injuries are mounting for the Rams, with the latest big one being that wide receiver Puka Nacua is heading to injured reserve, where he'll join Davante Adams, as Matthew Stafford is running out of healthy receivers.

If the Rams get healthy and make the playoffs, they'll be a major threat to any postseason opponent, which is why they still have the seventh-best odds in the league to win the Super Bowl at +1300.

But as the 49ers pull away in the NFC West, and the NFC wild card race looks increasingly competitive, the Rams' chances of being in it in January are dwindling.

item.title: Nick Sirianni denies giving subtle middle finger to fans
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After Sunday's loss to the Giants — Philadelphia's seventh loss in a row — a video emerged of Eagles coach Nick Sirianni leaving the field, along with Dom DiSandro.
item.content:encoded:
After Sunday's loss to the Giants — Philadelphia's seventh loss in a row — a video emerged of Eagles coach Nick Sirianni leaving the field, along with Dom DiSandro. It appeared, based on the manner in which Sirianni manipulated the fingers on his right hand, that he sent a one-fingered message to those who were heckling him.

Sirianni was asked about the apparent gesture during a Monday press conference.

"When [senior vice president of communications] Bob [Lange] told me that, absolutely not," Sirianni replied. "That was a surprise to me, but absolutely not."

Frankly, what else would Sirianni say? "Yes, it was a middle finger." If he admits it, he'll be fined — and the precedent for coaches is $100,000.

Beyond that, why would anyone believe him? Last Friday, Sirianni admitted that he misled reporters regarding the team's supposed commitment to quarterback Tanner McKee.

There's one other relevant factor, based on my own personal experience. My dad used to use that exact same move, during periodic verbal household disagreements with my mom.

I saw it. She never did. But that was the move. And, if she'd seen it, he would have denied it.

Just like Sirianni did.
